•81. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state:

(a) and (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir

*82. SHRI RAMACHANDRAIAH RUMANDLA:+ SHRI C. 
RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Station Ma ster of the oldest railway station at 
Shakkarnagar in Andhra Pradesh is never available for hearing grievances of the 
commuters; 
(b) if so whether the matter would be enquired into; and 
(c) the action taken to repair and renovate the station which is without any public 
amenities in working order? 
THE   MINISTER   OF   STATE   IN   THE   MINISTRY   OF 
The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Ramachandraiah Rumandia. 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2000] 
RAILWAYS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Shakkamagar is a small hah station on branch line of Nizamabad 
-Bodhan Metre Gauge section. Since there is no operational requirements for 
deploying Station Master, the station is managed by a 'Clerk-in-Charge* who remains 
on duty from 0600 hours to 1000 hours and 1700 hours to 2100 hours only as per train 
timings and is not available during the intervening period. Amenities commensurate 
with the volume of passengers dealt with have already been provided at the station. The 
face lifting of the station was done in Oct ober, 1999 and the existing building is in 
good condition. However, as a measure of augmenting the existing amenities, 
additional drinking water taps and seating arrangements are proposed to be provided. 
The approach road within the railway premises is also proposed to be black-topped.

[28 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Working of the Mid-day Meal Scheme 
*83. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have conducted any survey of the working of the 
Mid-day Meal Scheme for school children launched by Government in 1995; 
(b) if so, what are the findings of this survey report; and 
(c) what measures are being taken to plug the loopholes and deficiencies in 
implementation of the scheme as, revealed by the survey report? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) An evaluation has been undertaken in 10 States to assess the efficiency 
and effectiveness of the National Programme for Nutritional Support to Primary 
Education (Mid-Day Meals Scheme) by an independent agency, Operation Research 
Group, New Delhi. The study covers Assam, Gujarat, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, 
Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa,'Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The 
report was submitted in September, 1999. The findings of the report state that while 
the programme has given boost to enrolm ent in Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar 
Pradesh and West Bengal; in 6 other States  it has had positive impact on attendance 
and retention. 
Besides, a study conducted by NCERT on States policies on Incentive Schemes in 
Primary Schools and their Contribution to Girls' Participation, completed in April, 
2000, also covers the Mid-day Meal Scheme in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. The 
report states that the Noon Meal Scheme of Tamil Nadu and supply of food-grains 
under MDM in Uttar Pradesh have helped improve the enrolment and retention of girls 
in schools. 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2000] 
Based on the suggestions of the report and other feedback received from time to 
time, the Government has taken steps to improve the monitoring and supervision of the 
programme at all levels, create a greater awareness regarding the programme through 
involvement of Village Education Committees, streamline procedures so as to ensure 
regular supply of food-grains and timely reimbursement of transportation charges and 
payment to Food Corporation of India and ensure a more rigorous role for the nodal 
agency for programme implementation at the State level.

Statement 
(a) to (d) One normal coloured Tiger died in Nandankanan Zoo on 23rd June, 
2000. The postmortem reports confirme d that the animal died because of 
Trypanosomiasis, Another tiger showed symptoms of same sickness on 2nd July, 
2000. Therefore, the zoo authorities administ ered 'Berenil to 16 tigers of adjoining 
enclosures, after taking them into a squeezed cage. The animal which showed sign of 
sickness on 2nd July died on 4th July. Of the remaining 15 tigers which were 
administered drug on 3rd July, 8 tigers (six white and two coloured) died between 4th 
and 5th July, 2000. One white tiger each died on 6th and 7th July, 2000 respectively, ft 
has also been revealed that 5 tigers got infection of the same disease in 1999 of which 
3 died. One of the survivors of 1999 was amongst the 12 tigers died between 23rd June 
to 7th July 2000. 
The Central Government was informed of the deaths on the morning of 5th July, 
2000. The Ministry appointed an Expert Committee to find out the causes of death and 
to suggest ways and means to prevent recurrence of such happenings on 6th July, 
2000. The Committee was asked to start its work from 7th July and to give their report 
by 15th July, 2000. In the interim period the Ministry also decided to have an expert 
consultation to discuss the events at Nandankanan Zoo on 19th and 20th July, 2000. 
Union Ministry of Environment   and   Forests   officers   took   a   meeting  with   Chief

The reasons which might have led to flare up the disease were many ranging from 
over crowding of animals in the enclosures, ingress of livestock into the zoo because of 
breaches in the boundary wall, non-repair of  fencing of white tiger safari that was 
damaged by the cyclone, unhygienic method of feeding, poor drainage and increased 
vector loads due to bushes and shrubs in the vicinity of the enclosures. 
The Ministry is of the definite view that the response of zoo administration was 
inadequate to meet the situation. Zoo auth orities failed to take appropriate mitigative 
measures after the death of 3 tigers during 1999 from the same disease and again after 
the death of first tiger on 23rd June, 2000. No action was taken during this period for 
determining the parasitic loads in the bloo d of the tigers and providing prophylactic 
treatment to the animals between 23rd June to 2nd July, 2000. These views have been 
communicated to the State Govt, to take necessary disciplinary action against the 
persons responsible for the lapse. 
In consultation with the State Govt, detailed plan of action to tackle the situation 
has been worked out and the Ministry is monitoring the implementation of the action 
plan by the State Govt. closely.

*85. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will th e Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY

(b)' if so, whether Government are taking any steps in this regard; 
 whether Government have under consideration any other plan to control population;

 if so, the particulars thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. THAKUR): 
(a) to (d) India was among the first countries globally to launch a- National Family Welfare 
Programme, in 1952, with the objective of reducing birth rates to the extent necessary to 
stabilize the population at a level consistent with the requirement of national economy. In 
keeping with the democratic tradition of( the country, the family welfare programme seeks to: 
(w) promote responsible and planned parenthood through voluntary and informed choice 
of family planning methods best suited to individual acceptors, and 
(x) continue the target free approach in administering family planning services. 
We do not perceive that India needs compulsory sterilization. Our past experience indicates 
that it neither feasible nor desirable to put in place harsh or coercive measures for the 
promotion of compulsory sterilization. During 1970s, Family Welfare Programme focused 
primarily on terminal methods and received a setback on account of the rigid target based 
approach and coercion adopted during implementation. The Family Welfare Programme is 
today fully voluntary, target free and as well as need based. Our emphasis is on providing 
wider coverage and outreach of services

while   encouraging   citizens   through   information,   education   and communication to access 
the services and facilities provided. 
In particular remarkable progress has been made in the area of population stabilization in 
Kerala, Goa and Tamil Nadu without any coercion or compulsion. There is no proposal to make 
sterilization compulsory. 
The Government is extremely concerned about, improving the quality of life of its citizens 
by making reproductive health care accessible and affordable to all. besides also increasing the 
provision and outreach of primary and secondary education, extending basic amenities 
including sanitation, safe drinking water and housing, besides empowering women and 
enhancing their employment opportunities, and providing transport and communication. 
Accordingly, Government has recently taken the following steps: 
 1997 — Launched the Reproductive and Child Health Programme which has put in 
place the target free approach in the administration of Family Planning services. 
 February 2000 •— Adopted the National Population Policy 2000 which seeks to put in 
place an inter-sectoral agenda for achieving the goals and objectives of population 
stabilization. 
A large number of factors influence population growth rated and in turn are affected by it. 
Some of these factors are women's empowerment, women's status in the family, education 
particularly of women, and some other factors. Our actual success in containing the growth of 
population is dependent on: 
(i) Publicly stated support by the national level, state level and community level leaders; 
(ii) Efficiency and accountability within the State Health Systems for ensuring effective 
delivery of services to citizens; 
(iii) Women's education and women's status in the family; 
(iv) Resources assigned for population related programmes. 
Government has adopted a National Population Policy in February, 2000 which provides 
a holistic approach for achieving early

towards voluntary and informed choice and consent of citizens while availing of reproductive 
health care services, and continuation of the target free approach in administering family 
planning*services. It was laid on the Table of both Houses of Parliament during March, 2000. 
The immediate objective of the National Population Policy is to address the unmet needs of 
contraception, health infrastructure, health personnel and to provide integrated service delivery 
for basic reproductive and child health care. The medium term objective is to bring the total 
fertility rates to replacement level by 2010, through vigorous implementation of inter-sectoral 
operational strategics. 
In pursuance of these objectives, the following National Socio-Dcmographic Goals are 
enumerated for achievement by 2010: 
(1) Address the unmet needs for basic reproductive and child health services, supplies and 
infrastructure, (2) Make school education up to age 14 free and compulsory, and reduce 
drop outs at primary and secondary school levels to below 20 per cent for both boys and

maternal mortality ratio to below 100 per 100,000 live births, (5) Achieve universal 
immunization of children against all vaccine preventable diseases, (6) Promote delayed 
marriage for girls, not earlier than age 18 and preferably after 20 years of age, (7) Achieve 
80 per cent, institutional deliveries and 100 per cent deliveries by trained persons, (8) 
Achieve universal access to information counseling, and services for fertility regulation 
and contraception with a wide basket of choices, (9) Achieve 100 per cent registration of 
births, deaths, marriage and pregnancy, (10) Contain the spread of Acquired Immuno 
Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) and promote greater integration between the management 
of Reproductive Trace Infection (RTI) and Sexually Transmitted Infections (STI) and the 
National AIDS Control Organisation. (11) Prevent and control communicable diseases, 
(12) Integrate Indian System of Medicines (ISM) in the

630. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 what is the logic behind retaining the Retention Pricing Scheme (RPS) to provide 
subsidy; 
 whether it has proved effective in containing the prices and providing benefits to 
fertilizer consumers; 
 to whom the subsidy money goes-producers or the consumers of fertilizers and 
who gets how much; and

common man gets the maximum benefit? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAMESH BAIS): (a) Introduced on November 1, 1977, on the 
recommendations of "the Marathe Committee, Retention Price-eum-Subsidy Scheme 
has served the twin objectives of making urea available to farmers at affordable prices 
while ensuring the growth of fertilizer industry .by providing to the industry a fair and 
assured post tax return over the cost of production. 
 The farm gate prices of urea are fixed by the Government keeping in mind its 
affordability to the farmers. 
 While the farmers have to pay the notifie d farm gate price which is below iLe 
weighted average cost of production of the urea units, the scheme provides that the 
production units get their cost of production plus return as assured under the scheme. 
 Keeping in tune with the policy of economic liberalisation and reforms, all other 
fertilizers except urea have already been freed from 
64

price, movement and distribution control. The Government intends to move towards a 
de-regulatory regime in fertilizer sector in a phased manner after taking into account its 
fiscal capacity on the one hand and simultaneously making available fertilizers to the 
farmers at a reasonable price.

672. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: W ill the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
 whether it was mentioned at the WHO Conference in Amsterdam that 30 lakhs

 what steps Government intend to take to reduce the percentage of TB patients in

 whether Government have-conducted any study to completely eradicate TB from 
the country; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) and (b) It is estimated that about 
3 lakh children go out of school every year on account of their parents being affected by 
TB and India accounts for about 30% of TB patients in the world. 
(c) The National TB Control programme has been accorded high priority in India 
and is included under the 20-Point Programme. The main thrust is on early detection of 
the infectious sputum positive TB cases aid on treating them effectively. 
The Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) which aims at curing 85% 
of the new sputum positive cases and to detect at 
118 

[28th July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
least 70% of such cases, is at present in operation, and has covered more than 200 million 
population. It is expected that by 2002 about 500 million population will be covered under 
RNTCP. 
(d) and (e) There is no specific study regarding eradication of T.B. However, the National 
T.B. Control Programme was reviewed by a team of national and international experts in 1992. 
Based on their recommendations, Government of India evolved a revised programme, 
RNTCP, which was pilot tested in 1993, and expanded subsequently. In areas under RNTCP, 8 
out of 10 patients are being successfully treated compared to less than 4 out of 10 in the earlier 
programme and the death rate has been brought down 7 fold. A joint review of the RNTCP 
conducted in February, 2000 by Government of india and WHO has concluded that "RNTCP is 
being successfully implemented in India".

Lifting Ban on Non-Iodised Salt 
680. SHRr KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE-: Will the 
Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
 whether Government's attention has been drawn to the newsitem "Experts 
concerned over lifting of ban on non-iodised salt", appearing in the Asian Age dated 
17th June, 2000; 
 if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
 whether it is a fact that, as mentioned in the news-item, the Prime Minister has 
agreed to lift ban on the sale of non-iodised salt in the country; and 
(d) the reasons for disregarding the viewpoints of prominent 
scientific experts and health specialists all of whom have advised 
against the ban being lifted? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) Yes, Sir. 
 There is no ban on manufacture of non-iodised salt except the restriction on 
sale for direct human consumption. The notification issued on 10.5.2000 seeks public 
comments on a proposal to withdraw this restriction so that both iodised and 
non-iodised salt can be made available and the public can make an 'informed choice'. 
 and (d) No decision has yet been taken on the notification. Comments 
supporting and opposing the draft rules have been received from the public, including 
prominent scietific experts. All opinions received in the matter will be carefully 
considered before a final decision is taken. 
Withdrawal of Iodisation of Salt 
681. SHRI K.C. KONDAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) when iodisation of salt was made compulsory; 
130 

[28th July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether  it  is  a  fact  that   Government   have   issued  a 
preliminary    notification    proposing    withdrawal    of    compulsory iodisation of edible salt; 
 if so, the reasons for the proposed withdrawal; 
 whether it has come to the notice of Government that higher incidence of iodine 
deficiency disorders has been reported in many parts of the country, including Karnataka; and 
 whether Government would taken steps to drop the proposed withdrawal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA] ; (a) Sale of iodised salt for human 
consumption was made compulsory as per amendment made in PFA Rules, 1955 w.e.f. 
27.5.1998. 
(b) Yes, Sir. A notification publishing draft rules proposing 
removal of the restriction on sale of common salt for direct human 
consumption and inviting public comments was issued on 10.5.2000. 
 The decision to issue this notification was taken in the wake of sustained 
representations received from various sections of public, to the effect that the maters of public 
health should be left t the informed' choice of consumer and not enforced through compulsion. 
 As per surveys conducted in 282 districts in 25 States and 5 UTs including Karnataka, 
241 districts have been found to be endemic for IDD i.e. where the prevalence is more than 
10.0%, 
 Representations have been received from the public both supporting and opposing the 
proposed withdrawal of compulsory iodisation of salt for direct human consumption. All these 
representations will be carefully examined before a final decision is taken on whether to follow 
a strategy of compulsion or of voluntary acceptance of the use of iodised salt to combat iodine 
deficiency disorders.

An Enhanced Malaria Control Project is the Scheme for control of Malaria with a 
population of 4.9 million being covered by  it in 34 PHCs under 10 districts of 
Rajasthan. 
The criteria of inclusion of the PHC was: 
 Annual Parasite Incidence (API) of more than 2 for the last three years; 
 P. falciparum is more than 30% of malaria cases; 
 25% population of the PHC is tribal; and 
 The area has been reporting deaths due to malaria. 
There are four technical elements of the revised malaria control 
strategy: 
 to provide early diagnosis and prompt treatment; 
 to plan &  implement selective & sustainable preventive measures including 
vector control; 
 to detect early, contain or prevent epidemics; and 
 to strengthen local capacities in basic & applied research to permit & promote 
the regular assessment of a country's malaria situation, in particular the 
ecological, social and economic detriments of the disease.

and treatment of cancer, the cost of cancer management is costly.

colleges/Government supported Regional Cancer Centres, a large number of patients

by Registrar General of India under the sche me of Medical Certification of causes of 
death, cancer accounted for 3.5% of a!! deaths. It is estimated that cancer deaths may 
be 3 lakhs annually.

734. SHRIMATI CHANDRESH KUMARI: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have constituted some groups of women 
in the country since implementation of the Development of Women 
and Children in Rural Areas; 
 if so, details thereof with functions of the same; 
 whether Government propose to utilise these groups in other activities in case 
the objectives of DWCRA are achieved; and 
 if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) and (b) The scheme for 
Development for Women and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA) was in existence 
form 1982-83 to 1998-99 as a sub-scheme of Integrated Rural Development Programme 
(IRDP). From 1.4.1999, IRDP and its allied programme-including DWCRA were 
merged into the present self-employment programme i.e. Swarnjayanti Gram 
Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY). 
The primary objective of DWCRA was focussing attention on women members of 
the rural families below poverty line with a view to providing them opportunities of 
self-employment on a sustained basis. DWCRA thus focussed on providing income 
generating skill and activities to poor women in rural areas in order to improve their 
social and economic status. It also sought to encourage the. habit of thrift and credit 
among them. In addition, the programme aimed to enhance the welfare and quality of 
life of BPL family and community by improving the access of rural women to health, 
education, safe drinking wate r, sanitation, nutrition etc. A distinguishing feature of 
DWCRA was group strategy as against family as a unit of assistance under IRDP. The 
group strategy was adopted to motivate the rural women to come together and to break 
social bonds, which had denied them inco me generating and fulfilling opportunities. 
Each group comprised of about 10—-15 members which was provided a revolving   
fund   amounting   to   Rs.    15,000/-   upto   1994-95   and 
13_16GIPMR/2000 193 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2000] 
Rs. 25000/- from 1995-96. The fund was meant for the purpose of purchase of raw 
materials and marketing, honorarium to grou p organizer, infrastructure support for 
income generating and other group activities etc. The fund was shared equally by the 
Central Government and State Governments on 50-50 basis. In the case of Union 
Territories, Government of India provided cent per cent grant. (Prior to 1996-97, 
expenditure on Revolving Fund was shared between Central Government, State 
Government and UNICEF on 40:40:20 basis). 
Since inception upto 1998-99 a total of 2,72,722 groups were formed under 
DWCRA comprising 41,44,705 members. The central funds released to States/UTs 
during this period were Rs. 389,90 crore. 
(c) and (d) DWCRA groups of quality can be adopted in SGSY. The SGSY 
guidelines already provided for that. DRDAs have to put in concerted efforts to 
strengthen the groups formed under DWCRA during first year of SGSY.

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU) : Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, the Calling Attention motion on the death of animals in zoos and sanctuaries is 
evidence of the great empathy and concern that people in our country and Members of 
Parliament, in particular, have for wildlife. This will also send a clear and loud message to zoo 
and park managers that their performance is being closely watched by the nation and that their 
response to the mandate given to them has to be appropriate and adequate. Even before I 
received notice of this Calling Attention motion, I had proposed to seek leave to make a 
statement on the recent death of zoo tigers. 
I have personally monitored factors relating to the death of twelve tigers at 
Nandankanan 200. i have no reserv ation in admitting that th e zoo director and the zoo 
veterinarian were unable to show the professional competence that was expected of them. A 
number of significant inadequacies have been identified and the State Government has been 
requested to take mitigative measures. Overcrowding of anima !s, inappropriate housing, poor 
standards of sanitation and hygiene and inadequate expertise in the field of health care of zoo 
animals have jointly contributed to these deaths. Another negative factor has been the 
inadequate level of funding that the zoo has received from the State Government in the past 
years. 
Then I received information of some other upsetting incidents. The recent deaths of 
lions in Gir, cheetals in Ranthambore and peacocks at Morena were also enquired into. 
The information that I have is that except for one lion that was 
electrocuted, the death of the other lions was because of natural causes and currently there is 
no threat of any kind of infection to other animals in the area. As regards the death of cheetahs in 
Ranthambore, a few animals were killed by dogs in the fringe areas of the Park, whilst two 
animals were suffering from tuberculosis. ! will have something more to say on this later. in 
Morena district, investigations revealed that a number of peacocks died due to consumption of 
bajra seed which had been treated with pesticides. 
I would like to give some statistics about existing zoos. Presently, there are 199 
recognised zoos, of which 15 are large, 17 medium, 31 small 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [28 JULY, 2000)  
and 136 mini zoos and deer parks. The total number of animals in these zoos, which includes 
birds and reptiles, is around 25,000. Of this, 9000 animals belong to the endangered category. 
According to the information available with me, during the last four years, around 1600 animals 
have died in these zoos, which comes to about 10 per cent of the tola!. 
As regards tigers, their number in zoos is around 313. More than 75 per cent of the 
tigers are of captive-bred origin. No tiger has been captured in the last ten years for the purpose 
of display in the zoos. The number of tigers that have died between 1995-96 and 1998-99 is 141. 
Of this, tigers account for an average of 35 deaths in a year. This is about 12 per cent of the 
population of zoo tigers. The average birth rate of tigers during this period is about 19 per cent. 
As regards the number of wild animal deaths in sanctuaries approximately, 140 tigers, 
700 panthers, 450 elephants, 15 lions, and 127 rhinoceros have been killed by poachers in the 
last five years. 
In the wild, we have an estimated population of tigers, which is between 3500 and 
3700. Taking the average life span of tigers as 20 years, out of this population, not less than 176 
tigers would be dying of old age. There is the incidence of infant mortality also and about 400 
cubs die a natural death every year. Then, mere are instances of handicapped animals dying of 
starvation, as well as tigers killing each other to safeguard their territory. 
An area of concern that I would like to bring to the notice of the hon. Members is the 
negative impact of disturbances in the habitat of the animals and the inadequate prey base of the 
cats. This has resulted in a tendency on the part of tigers and other cats to increasingly look 
towards livestock to meet their food requirements. This has led to a man and animal conflict, with 
resultant instances of poisoning. 
The panther appears to be under greater threat because of its tendency to live in the 
fringe areas of the forest. Intrusions by panther into human habitation is not uncommon, where 
they are lured by easy prey availability of livestock: dogs and, at times, human infants. In this 
regard, the position tends to become quite grim at times in the hills of Himachal Pradesh and 
Uttar pradesh. There have also been instances of panther intrust ion into some  suburbs of 
Bombay and within the limits of Guwahati City.     Recently, in a series of seizures,  200 panther 
skins and a larger

[28 JULY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
number of other parts such as nails were seized. While the regulatory agencies have been put 
on the alert, these cases have been referred to the CBI. Separately, my Ministry is in the process 
of finalizing a proposal for an exclusive agency to investigate - wild life crimes. There are, 
however, other issues also. .We have made arrangements for increase in compensation for 
cattle deaths as also for speedy disbursement of compensation. Besides, a greater degree of 
awareness is also needed to sensitize those who are involved in man and animal conflicts about 
the precious loss to our biodiversity when needless senselessness takes place in such 
situations. My Ministry is working on a scheme to increase the level of public awareness in this 
area. 
I would like to mention that epidemics also take a heavy toll of wild animal life. 
Sometime around 1950, 30 to 40 per cent of the wild ass population was wiped out due to 
trypanosomiasis. In the seve nties, an outbreak of rinderpe st nearly wiped out the gaur 
population in Madumalai, parts of Periyar and Bandipur. Fortunately, nature has been able to 
revive the depleted population', assisted by availably of an adequate habitat and effective 
protection measures. 
Another important issue is the destruction of wild life habitats. Habitat destruction due 
to biotic pressures and various developmental activities have brought down the recruitment rate, 
especially in the case of the  tiger.      Sharing  of common  grazing   grounds  and  water  pool   
with 
livestock has brought in diseases like tuberculosis in national parks and sanctuaries. Cases of 
tuberculosis in tigers have been reported from Sariska in Rajasthan. 
Railway lines passing through forests continue to be a serious threat for elephants. 
Five elephants in Uttar Pradesh and six in Assam have died because of this reason. Road 
accidents have also taken a toll of wild animals in Kaziranga, Assam and Gir in Gujarat, 
I will be failing in my duty if ! do not mention that the draining of 
water bodies and swamps for agricultural purposes has severely affected the population of 
swamp deer and various species of water birds. Intensive agriculture and deforestation in high 
hill areas has intensified floods in our major rivers. The Kaziranga National Park is a regular 
victim of such floods. The Hoods in 1998 monsoons took a toll of two tigers, forty-four rhinos, 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [28 JULY, 2000]  
three elephants, three wild buffalos, fifty swamp deer and more than six hundred herbivores. 
There are reports of three elephants being washed away in flood waters in West Bengal, Use of 
pesticides has added another serious dimension to the problem. We are ail worried about fifty 
peacocks dying after eating bajra seeds coated with pesticide. I am informed that twelve 
elephants died in Dhenkanal district of Orissa because of consumption of agricultural crop 
which had been sprayed with pesticide by the farmers. Experience over the years has brought 
about a realization that wild animal population cannot be preserved only -in isolated islands of 
national parks and sanctuaries. Wild animals know no legal boundaries, We will have to adopt a 
total, landscape approach for protection of wildlife. Farmers will have to be convinced to adopt 
cropping patterns under which the damage to crops from wild animals is minimal. 
We are trying to ensure increased allocations to the State Governments, expeditious 
flow of funds, strengthening of protection-infrastructure, creation of a specialized agency for 
monitoring and collection of intelligence data on poaching and seeking international 
cooperation for curbing trans-border trade. However, the success in wild life conservation will 
be limited unless people from all walks of life cooperate in tackling the problems of poverty in the 
vicinity of national parks and sanctuaries, through ecologically - sustainable development 
strategies. The use of chemical pesticides and fertilizers will have to give way to use of organic 
manure and bio-pesticides in the vicinity of wild life habitats. Treating the scrub forests as 
wastelands and diverting them for agriculture, draining every drop of water for irrigation will 
have to stop. All this can be achieved by reviving the healthy tradition of this country of living in 
harmony with nature. Willd life conservation has to be the concern of all departments of the 
Government at Centre and State level. Ecological security should get the same priority as is 
given for national security. I hope that the debate we have on this very important subject will 
give us greater strength to effectively meet the challenge of conserving our biological diversity.
